fields.title: Kedr: Competitor Announces Price Twice as Low
fields.summary: Sales demands discounts, development wants to catch up on features. Decide on the strategy for the half-year.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you propose to the board of directors for the upcoming half-year?
fields.brief/company: Kedr is a fictional cloud warehouse management service for small distributors. 120 customers, average bill of 40 thousand rubles per month, sales cycle of two months.
fields.brief/context: A major competitor, Yarus, has announced a cloud version for 19 thousand per month. Sales demands a price cut, development proposes catching up on features. In six months, you must defend your plan before the board of directors.
fields.brief/objective: Decide what to do in the upcoming half-year.
fields.brief/constraints: Team of 14. No budget for a sharp increase in expenses: the company runs on its own revenue.
fields.brief/task: Choose a direction and justify it.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Respond to the mechanism, not the price list
fields.learnTakeaway/body: A competitor's announced price is just the tip of their business model: one includes implementation, another sells it separately, a third gets customers from partners for a revenue share. Until you dissect the mechanism, any response will miss the mark. Your own decisions should be verified with two tables: profit by segment after deducting support costs, and price arithmetic with acceptable churn.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
120 customers, 4.8 million ₽ per month. Profit breakdown after deducting support and custom development:

Distributors with 15–40 employees, single warehouse, standard processes: 31 customers, 62% of profit, about 20 minutes of support per month.

Medium distributors: 68 customers, 41% of profit, about an hour of support per month.

Chains with multiple warehouses: 12 customers, paying three times the average but requiring custom development—generating a net loss in total.

Manufacturing companies: 9 customers, the product doesn't cover their processes, average lifetime of 5 months, one-third of all support tickets.

Annual churn: 14 customers, 7 of whom are manufacturing companies.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Cloud version is 19 thousand per month. Implementation is sold separately and costs 300 thousand; in the first year, a customer pays more than they would with us.

About 60% of Yarus's customers come from eight integration partners who are paid 20% of the first year's revenue. We don't have a partner program.

Customers rarely leave Yarus: three years of data and trained staff make switching expensive.

Yarus's implementation time is two weeks. We did 34 implementations this year, averaging 3.4 days.

Meanwhile, half of our lost deals go to 'staying on Excel for now' rather than to Yarus: 16 out of 27 closed-lost deals this year.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Starting September 1, mandatory labeling is extended to two more product groups. In our database, this affects 40% of customers and most prospects.

We don't support labeling; development estimate is 8 weeks.

Yarus has labeling, but it is included only in their expensive tier.

The key interest rate has risen; distributors are cutting inventory and delaying implementations. Our sales cycle has grown from two months to two and a half over the last six months.

Over the year, we lost 11 deals due to the lack of integration with two popular accounting systems. Each integration is estimated at 5 weeks.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Sales: lower the price to 25 thousand, otherwise 'we are compared and we lose.' They also ask to allow a 30% discount for the first year.

Development: close the feature gap with Yarus over the next six months—multi-warehouse support, reports, roles. Estimate: the entire team for the whole half-year.

Founder: 'let's expand into manufacturing companies, there's more money there.'

Marketing: create a comparison page with Yarus.

None of these proposals are backed by calculations.

There has been no price increase for three years, despite noticeable inflation during this time.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Focus on the profitable segment and meet the labeling deadline
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Reorganize operations around the profitable segment, release labeling support before September 1, leverage our implementation speed, and either drop or reprice unprofitable segments.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
The profit breakdown changes the conversation: 31 customers generate 62% of profit, while chains and manufacturing companies drain it. The founder's proposal about manufacturing is dismissed with a single table showing a 5-month customer lifetime and one-third of support tickets.
You release labeling support on August 20: 40% of the customer base is required to upgrade, and Yarus only offers it in their expensive tier. This brings in 19 new customers in the fall, all from the profitable segment.
You turn implementation speed into a key argument: 3.4 days vs two weeks, which is critical before September 1.
You raise prices for chains by 60%: four leave, the rest become profitable. You stop selling to manufacturing companies.
You don't lower the price; instead, for the first time in three years, you raise it by 15% for new customers.
Six months later, revenue is up 21% with the same number of customers, and support is relieved.
Trade-off: integrations are not built, so you will continue to lose 11 similar deals a year—this was a conscious delay.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Lower the price to match Yarus
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: We are compared on price and we lose. Drop the price to 25 thousand and allow a 30% discount for the first year.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
New deals increase by a quarter, and sales is happy.
However, revenue drops: 120 customers with an average bill of 27 thousand bring in 3.24 million instead of 4.8 million. Almost no profit is left.
The price comparison was false from the start: Yarus charges 300 thousand separately for implementation, meaning a customer pays more in the first year than with us—no one verified this argument.
Existing customers find out about the new price and demand contract renegotiations.
Six months later, there is not enough budget for the September 1 labeling release, and the window of opportunity closes.
Trade-off: you entered a price war with a competitor who has a larger safety margin, and wasted your only timeline advantage on it.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Development is right: Yarus has more features. Dedicate the entire team for six months to multi-warehouse support, reports, and roles.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
By March, the gap is indeed narrower, and the presentation looks convincing.
But this barely adds any customers: 60% of Yarus's customers come from eight integration partners rather than choosing from a feature list. Their growth mechanism is the channel, and it remains untouched.
Multi-warehouse support is needed by chains—the segment that is unprofitable for us; thus, the team spent six months working for customers who bring in a net loss.
Labeling is not ready by September 1, and 40% of the customer base leaves to upgrade with competitors who have it.
Trade-off: you analyzed the competitor by their storefront instead of their growth mechanism, spending half a year playing catch-up where it wasn't needed.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Raise the price and focus on monetization
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Prices haven't been raised for three years. Raise them by 15%, work on expansion within existing customers, and ignore the competitor.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The arithmetic is correct: with a 15% price increase, it only becomes unprofitable if more than 13% of customers churn, whereas market experience shows 3–6% churn. Revenue grows by 9% with almost no effort.
This is the best of the quick fixes and protects against a price war.
However, the price increase is flat for everyone: manufacturing companies and chains remain, continuing to drain support, while some profitable small customers hit a budget ceiling.
Labeling is not released—the team was busy with pricing tiers—and the autumn window of opportunity is missed.
Trade-off: the right lever was pulled without segmentation and without considering the deadline, which was the only window of opportunity for the half-year.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: An external factor was identified but not carried through to its implications for the decision
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: A strength was claimed without proof and without identifying what it constrains
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: The competitor was analyzed by their feature set rather than their growth mechanism
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Customers were not segmented by profit and support cost
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: A financial decision was made without the arithmetic of pricing, churn, and expansion
